connection: Session 14 studied a type constraint on a generic method. This session studies a different kind of generic type parameter behavior -- variance -- using ISource<out T> and ISink<in T>, two new, small interfaces built specifically to make covariance and contravariance observable, since nothing in the real domain's own interfaces uses either.
objectives: Explain what out on ISource<out T> permits: treating an ISource<Employee> as an ISource<object> safely.
Explain what in on ISink<in T> permits: treating an ISink<object> as an ISink<Employee> safely.
Predict, and confirm, which of the two assignments (ISource<Employee> to ISource<object>, or the reverse) compiles.

Explain why neither IClockEntryRepository nor IClockEntryService uses variance annotations -- their type parameters, where they exist, don't create a supertype/subtype relationship that variance would apply to.

visuals.title: out permits widening the output type
visuals.explanation: ISource<Employee> source = ...; ISource<object> widened = source; -- legal because ISource<out T> only ever produces (returns) a T, never accepts one.

visuals.title: in permits narrowing the input type
visuals.explanation: ISink<object> sink = ...; ISink<Employee> narrowed = sink; -- legal because ISink<in T> only ever accepts (consumes) a T as a parameter, never returns one.

visuals.title: The direction of data flow decides which variance is safe
visuals.explanation: A type that only produces T can safely be treated as producing something less specific (object); a type that only consumes T can safely be treated as consuming something more specific.

visuals.title: Real repository interfaces have no supertype/subtype relationship to vary over
visuals.explanation: IClockEntryRepository is not generic over Employee/object the way ISource<T> is -- there is no ClockEntry-vs-object substitution question for variance to answer there.

preQuiz.prompt: Given ISource<Employee> employeeSource = new SingleSource<Employee>(someEmployee);, does ISource<object> objectSource = employeeSource; compile?
options: Yes -- ISource<out T> is covariant: because it only ever returns a T (via Get()), an ISource<Employee> can safely stand in anywhere an ISource<object> is expected
No -- generic interfaces never allow this kind of assignment
preQuiz.explanation: out T marks ISource as covariant in T specifically because Get() only produces a T -- there is no method that could misuse the wider object type to insert something Employee-incompatible.

preQuiz.prompt: Given ISink<object> objectSink = new CountingSink<object>();, does ISink<Employee> employeeSink = objectSink; compile?
options: Yes -- ISink<in T> is contravariant: because it only ever accepts a T (via Add(T)), an ISink<object> can safely stand in anywhere an ISink<Employee> is expected, since it can accept an Employee (an object) just fine
preQuiz.explanation: in T marks ISink as contravariant specifically because Add only consumes a T -- an ISink<object> is willing to accept anything, including an Employee, so it satisfies an ISink<Employee> contract.

preQuiz.prompt: Why doesn't IClockEntryRepository use out or in anywhere?
options: Its members mix production and consumption of ClockEntry (SaveClockEntry takes one in; GetClockEntry/GetEmployeeClockEntries return them) -- a type that both produces and consumes T cannot safely be marked variant in either direction
IClockEntryRepository is not a generic interface
Variance only applies to interfaces with exactly one method
preQuiz.explanation: IClockEntryRepository is a plain, non-generic interface -- ClockEntry is a concrete parameter/return type throughout, not a type parameter T. There is nothing to mark out or in.

concept.title: out T: safe when a type only produces T
paragraphs: ISource<out T> { T Get(); } has exactly one member, and it only returns a T -- it never accepts a T as an argument anywhere.

Because of that one-directional shape, the compiler allows ISource<Employee> to be used wherever ISource<object> is expected: anything you could do with an ISource<object> (call Get() and get back some object) still works when the object happens to be an Employee.

concept.title: in T: safe when a type only consumes T
paragraphs: ISink<in T> { void Add(T item); } has exactly one member, and it only accepts a T -- it never returns one.

Because it never hands a T back out, an ISink<object> (which can Add any object at all) can stand in for an ISink<Employee> (which only ever needs to Add Employee objects) -- accepting a wider type is always safe when nothing depends on getting a narrower type back.

concept.title: Real repository interfaces are neither -- and that's expected
paragraphs: IClockEntryRepository's SaveClockEntry(ClockEntry) consumes a ClockEntry; GetClockEntry and GetEmployeeClockEntries produce ClockEntry values. A single interface mixing both directions over the same type parameter cannot be safely marked out or in -- the compiler would reject either annotation if attempted.

This is not a gap in the real code -- IClockEntryRepository is not even generic over ClockEntry (ClockEntry is a fixed, concrete type in its signatures, not a type parameter). Variance only becomes a question once a type is generic and used consistently in one direction.

lab.objective: Confirm ISource<out T>'s covariant assignment and ISink<in T>'s contravariant assignment compile, and confirm the reverse direction of each does not.
lab.startingCondition: ISource<T>, ISink<T>, SingleSource<T>, and CountingSink<T> already exist with their real variance annotations.
steps: Assign an ISource<Employee> to an ISource<object> variable and confirm it compiles.
Attempt to assign an ISource<object> to an ISource<Employee> variable and confirm the compiler rejects it.
Assign an ISink<object> to an ISink<Employee> variable and confirm it compiles.
Attempt to assign an ISink<Employee> to an ISink<object> variable and confirm the compiler rejects it.
lab.expectedBehavior: ISource<Employee> -> ISource<object> and ISink<object> -> ISink<Employee> both compile; the reverse of each does not.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

expectedFiles.why: Confirm the real ISource<out T>/ISink<in T> declarations and their implementations.
Confirm both variance directions are covered.
Publish synchronized lesson, lab, and quiz material.

commit: session-15: teach variance at api boundaries
review: Both variance directions are demonstrated with actual assignments, not just described in prose.
The reverse (invalid) direction of each is confirmed to genuinely fail to compile, not merely asserted.
IClockEntryRepository's lack of variance annotations is explained honestly, connecting back to its real, mixed-direction, non-generic signature shape.

postQuiz.prompt: Could IEnumerable<T> (Session 12) be marked out T, the way ISource<T> is?
options: Yes -- IEnumerable<T> is actually declared IEnumerable<out T> in .NET, for the same reason as ISource<T>: it only ever produces T values (via GetEnumerator/Current), never accepts them
postQuiz.explanation: This is a real fact about the .NET base class library, not just this course's example -- IEnumerable<out T>'s real covariance is exactly why IEnumerable<ClockEntry> could be assigned to an IEnumerable<object> variable if needed.

postQuiz.prompt: Why would attempting to add an out T marker to ISink<T> (making it ISink<out T>) fail to compile?
options: Add(T item) takes T as an input parameter -- out (covariance) requires T to appear only in output positions, and a parameter is an input position
out T is only valid on interfaces with more than one member
It would compile, but behave unpredictably at runtime
postQuiz.explanation: C# actually enforces this at compile time: an out type parameter cannot appear in an input (parameter) position anywhere in the interface -- the compiler catches the mismatch between the requested variance and the interface's real shape.

postQuiz.prompt: If IClockEntryRepository someday became generic (say, IRepository<T> shared across ClockEntry and Employee), could it be marked out T?
options: No -- as long as it has a method like Save(T item) that accepts a T as a parameter, it cannot be covariant; consuming and producing the same type parameter in one interface rules out both variance directions
Yes, automatically, once it becomes generic
Only if T is a value type
postQuiz.explanation: This is the same structural reason IClockEntryRepository has no variance today -- any interface that both takes T in and hands T back out cannot be safely marked variant in either direction.

reflections: Why did this session need a new, purpose-built pair of interfaces (ISource<T>/ISink<T>) instead of finding variance already at work in the real domain?
Where in the .NET base class library (beyond IEnumerable<out T>) have you seen a variance-annotated generic interface, now that you know what to look for?
If Employee eventually implemented some IEmployeeLike interface, what would need to be true about ISource<Employee> for it to also be usable as an ISource<IEmployeeLike>?
whatBreaks: Attempting to declare ISource<T> as out T while also giving it a method that accepts a T parameter would fail to compile -- the compiler enforces that out type parameters appear only in output positions. Assigning an ISource<object> to an ISource<Employee> variable (the unsafe direction) correctly fails to compile, because nothing guarantees every object produced by that source is actually an Employee.
summary: ISource<out T> is safely covariant because its one member only produces T; ISource<Employee> can stand in for ISource<object> as a result. ISink<in T> is safely contravariant because its one member only consumes T; ISink<object> can stand in for ISink<Employee>. IClockEntryRepository has no variance annotations because its real methods both consume ClockEntry (SaveClockEntry) and produce it (GetClockEntry, GetEmployeeClockEntries) -- a shape variance cannot safely apply to, and (more fundamentally) because it isn't generic over ClockEntry at all.
